question: What are the three pillars of observability (logs, metrics, traces), and what does each tell you?

key_points: Logs: detailed, timestamped records of discrete events — great for understanding exactly what happened at a specific point, but expensive to store/search at scale and easy to over-log or under-log
Metrics: numeric time-series measurements (request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, CPU usage) — cheap to store and great for dashboards/alerting on trends, but lack per-request detail
Traces: follow a single request's journey across multiple services, showing where time was spent at each hop — essential for diagnosing latency issues in distributed/microservices systems
Together they complement each other: metrics alert you something's wrong, traces pinpoint where in the request path, logs give the exact detail of what happened there
reference_solution.sample_answer: Logs are detailed, timestamped records of discrete events, giving you the exact detail of what happened at a specific point in time, but they're comparatively expensive to store and search at scale, and it's easy to either drown in noise or miss the one line that mattered. Metrics are numeric time-series measurements — things like request rate, error rate, or latency percentiles — which are cheap to store and great for dashboards and alerting on trends over time, but they don't give you per-request detail. Traces follow a single request's journey across multiple services in a distributed system, showing exactly where time was spent at each hop, which is essential for diagnosing latency problems that logs and metrics alone can't localize. In practice they complement each other in an investigation: a metric alert tells you something's wrong, a trace helps pinpoint where in the request path it's happening, and logs from that specific span give you the precise detail of what actually occurred there.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to walk through diagnosing a sudden latency spike using all three signals together.

question: What is the difference between monitoring and observability?

key_points: Monitoring: watching for known failure modes you've anticipated in advance, via predefined dashboards/alerts (is CPU high? is the error rate above X?)

Observability: the ability to ask arbitrary new questions about the system's internal state from its external outputs, WITHOUT having predicted that specific question in advance — useful for debugging novel, previously unseen failure modes
Monitoring answers 'is something wrong' for known scenarios; observability supports answering 'why is this specific unusual thing happening' for scenarios nobody explicitly built a dashboard for
Rich, structured, high-cardinality telemetry (not just a handful of predefined dashboards) is what makes a system observable versus merely monitored
reference_solution.sample_answer: Monitoring is about watching for known failure modes you've anticipated in advance, using predefined dashboards and alert thresholds — like alerting when CPU usage crosses 90% or the error rate exceeds some percentage. Observability is a broader capability: the ability to ask arbitrary new questions about what's happening inside the system, from its external telemetry, without having predicted that specific question ahead of time — which matters when you're debugging a genuinely novel failure mode nobody built a specific dashboard for. So monitoring is good at answering 'is something wrong' for scenarios you expected, while observability is what lets you answer 'why is this weird, unexpected thing happening' by slicing and querying rich, structured telemetry data in ways you didn't pre-plan. Having lots of dashboards doesn't automatically make a system observable — what matters is whether the underlying telemetry has enough detail and structure to support answering questions you haven't thought of yet.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to describe a real debugging scenario where pre-built dashboards weren't enough and they needed to query raw, high-cardinality telemetry instead.

question: What is a good alerting strategy to avoid alert fatigue?

key_points: Alert fatigue: too many low-value or noisy alerts cause on-call engineers to start ignoring or desensitizing to alerts, including important ones — the boy who cried wolf problem
Alert on symptoms that actually affect users (SLO/error budget burn, elevated error rates, latency) rather than every possible internal metric anomaly
Every alert that fires should be actionable — if there's nothing a human can/should do about it, it shouldn't page anyone; route it to a dashboard or a lower-urgency channel instead
Use appropriate thresholds and durations (avoid alerting on a single noisy data point; require sustained conditions) and clear runbooks so responders know what to do once paged
reference_solution.sample_answer: Alert fatigue happens when too many low-value or noisy alerts fire, causing on-call engineers to start ignoring or tuning out alerts altogether, including the genuinely important ones — that's dangerous since it defeats the whole purpose of alerting. A good strategy is to alert primarily on symptoms that actually affect users — like SLO or error-budget burn rate, elevated user-facing error rates, or latency crossing a meaningful threshold — rather than paging on every internal metric fluctuation that might just be normal noise. Every alert that pages someone should be genuinely actionable — if there's nothing a human needs to or can do about it right now, it shouldn't wake anyone up; route that instead to a dashboard or a lower-urgency notification channel. I'd also make sure thresholds require a sustained condition rather than firing on one noisy data point, and that every alert has a clear runbook so whoever gets paged knows what to actually do, rather than starting an investigation from scratch every time.

follow_up_hint: Ask them what an 'error budget' is and how it can be used to decide when to actually page someone versus let a minor issue accumulate.
